lessons.title: Calculating the Cost of Producing One Jar or Sachet
lessons.body: To know if you are making a profit, you must first know exactly how much it costs to produce one jar or sachet of tomato paste or sauce. This is called your unit cost. Start by listing every ingredient and material you use for one batch. For example, to make 50 jars of tomato paste, you might use 20 kg of fresh tomatoes at 500 CFA per kg, 2 kg of onions at 400 CFA per kg, 1 litre of oil at 800 CFA, 0.5 kg of salt at 300 CFA, 0.2 kg of spices at 1,000 CFA, and 50 jars with lids at 100 CFA each. Add the cost of fuel or electricity for cooking, and labour if you pay someone. Let's calculate: tomatoes = 10,000 CFA; onions = 800 CFA; oil = 800 CFA; salt = 150 CFA; spices = 200 CFA; jars = 5,000 CFA; fuel = 1,000 CFA; labour = 2,000 CFA. Total batch cost = 19,950 CFA. Divide by 50 jars to get cost per jar: 19,950 Ã· 50 = 399 CFA per jar. Always round up to 400 CFA to be safe. If you also use labels, add that cost. For sachets, do the same but count sachets per batch. Remember to include a small amount for spoilage or wastage, say 5%. So add 5% of 400 = 20 CFA, making unit cost 420 CFA. You must recalculate whenever prices change. Keep a notebook with these numbers. This unit cost is the foundation for setting your price.

lessons.title: Setting a Selling Price that Covers Costs and Gives Profit
lessons.body: Once you know your unit cost, you can set a selling price that covers all costs and gives you a profit. The simplest method is cost-plus pricing. Decide on a profit marginâa percentage added to your unit cost. For example, if your unit cost is 420 CFA per jar, and you want a 30% profit margin, multiply 420 by 1.30 to get 546 CFA. You might round to 550 CFA. But you must also check what customers are willing to pay. Go to local markets and see the price of similar tomato paste. If competitors sell at 500 CFA, you may need to reduce your margin or find ways to lower your cost. Another method is to work backwards: if the market price is 500 CFA, and you want 20% profit, your maximum cost must be 500 Ã· 1.20 = 416 CFA. If your cost is higher, you must reduce costs or accept lower profit. Always consider your target customers: in low-income areas, small sachets at 50 CFA may sell better than large jars. Calculate the price per gram or per serving to compare. Don't forget to include a little extra for transport to market and market fees. For example, if transport adds 10 CFA per jar, your total cost becomes 430 CFA, so at 550 CFA your profit is 120 CFA per jar. Write down your price and review it every few months. Never sell below your unit cost, even to friends. A simple rule: price = unit cost + desired profit + selling expenses.

lessons.title: Keeping Simple Records of Sales and Expenses
lessons.body: Keeping records is not optional if you want your food business to grow. You don't need a computer or expensive software. A simple exercise book and a pen are enough. Divide the book into two sections: one for sales and one for expenses. Every time you sell a jar or sachet, write the date, quantity sold, and amount received. For example: '5 Jan 2025, 10 jars, 5,500 CFA'. Every time you buy ingredients or pay for fuel, write it in the expenses section: '5 Jan 2025, tomatoes 20 kg, 10,000 CFA'. At the end of each day, total your sales and expenses. At the end of the week, add up all sales and all expenses. Subtract expenses from sales to get your profit or loss. Keep all receipts in a small envelope or plastic bag. If you sell on credit, write the customer's name and amount owed in a separate 'debts' list. Follow up weekly. Also record your inventory: how many jars you have left, how many tomatoes in stock. This helps you know when to buy more. At the end of the month, review your records to see which products sell best and which expenses are highest. You can then adjust. Many small businesses fail because they mix personal money with business money. Open a separate bank account or mobile money wallet for the business. Pay yourself a small salary from the business, but record it as an expense. Good records help you get loans from microfinance institutions, because they can see you are serious.

lessons.title: Managing Cash Flow for a Small Food Business
lessons.body: Cash flow is the movement of money in and out of your business. Even if you are making a profit on paper, you can run out of cash if you don't manage it well. For example, you might sell 100 jars on credit, meaning you have 'sales' but no cash to buy more tomatoes. To manage cash flow, follow these rules: First, encourage cash sales. Offer a small discount for immediate payment, like 5% off. Second, if you must sell on credit, set a clear payment date and follow up. Third, keep a cash reserve for emergencies and for buying raw materials when prices are low. Aim to have enough cash to cover at least one month's expenses. Fourth, buy ingredients in bulk when you have cash, but don't tie up all your cash in stock. Fifth, pay your suppliers on time to maintain good relationships, but negotiate for credit if possible. Sixth, separate your personal wallet from the business cash box. At the end of each day, count your cash and compare it to your records. If you are short, find out why. Use a simple cash flow forecast: list expected cash inflows (sales, loans) and outflows (ingredients, labour, transport) for the next month. This helps you see if you will have enough cash. For example, if you expect to sell 500 jars at 550 CFA each, that's 275,000 CFA. If your expenses are 200,000 CFA, you have a surplus of 75,000 CFA. But if half your sales are on credit, you only have 137,500 CFA cash, which may not cover expenses. So plan accordingly. Always keep a small buffer.

lessons.title: Understanding Break-Even Point
lessons.body: The break-even point is the number of jars or sachets you must sell to cover all your costsâboth fixed and variableâwithout making a profit or a loss. Fixed costs are expenses that don't change with production, like rent for your kitchen, a license, or a monthly loan payment. Variable costs change with each unit produced, like tomatoes, jars, and labour. To calculate break-even, first find your unit selling price and unit variable cost. Suppose you sell a jar for 550 CFA. Your variable cost per jar (ingredients, packaging, fuel) is 420 CFA. Your contribution margin per jar is 550 - 420 = 130 CFA. This 130 CFA goes towards covering your fixed costs. If your fixed costs per month are 50,000 CFA (rent, license, etc.), then break-even = fixed costs Ã· contribution margin = 50,000 Ã· 130 = 385 jars. So you must sell at least 385 jars per month to break even. If you sell more, you make a profit; if less, you make a loss. You can also calculate break-even in sales revenue: fixed costs Ã· (contribution margin Ã· selling price) = 50,000 Ã· (130/550) = 50,000 Ã· 0.236 = 211,538 CFA. So you need 211,538 CFA in sales to break even. Knowing your break-even helps you set sales targets. If you think you can only sell 300 jars, you might reduce fixed costs (e.g., work from home) or increase contribution margin (raise price or reduce variable costs). Review your break-even every month as costs change. Use a simple calculator or notebook. This number is your survival lineânever go below it for long.

lessons.title: Avoiding Common Money Mistakes in Food Processing
lessons.body: Many small food processors make the same money mistakes that kill their businesses. Here are the most common and how to avoid them. First, not separating business and personal money. You buy tomatoes with the same wallet you use for school fees. Then you can't tell if you made a profit. Solution: open a separate mobile money account or bank account for the business. Pay yourself a fixed salary. Second, underpricing. You calculate cost as only ingredients, forgetting fuel, labour, and packaging. Then you sell at a price that doesn't cover everything. Always use the full unit cost method. Third, not keeping records. Without records, you don't know your best-selling product or biggest expense. Keep a daily sales and expense book. Fourth, buying too much stock. You see tomatoes on sale and buy 100 kg, but they spoil before you use them. Buy only what you need for a week or two. Fifth, selling on credit without follow-up. You give 50 jars to a shop on credit, but you never collect the money. Set clear terms and follow up weekly. Sixth, mixing loans with personal use. You borrow for the business but spend it on a family event. Use loans only for business expenses. Seventh, not saving for emergencies. When your cooker breaks, you have no money to repair it. Save at least 5% of sales each week. Eighth, ignoring taxes and licenses. You may face fines later. Check local regulations. Ninth, not tracking break-even. You might be busy but still losing money. Calculate break-even monthly. Tenth, spending all profit on personal items. Reinvest at least 30% of profit into the business to grow. Avoid these mistakes and your tomato paste business will be stronger.

quiz.q: What is the unit cost of a product?
options: A) The total cost of all ingredients in one batch
B) The cost of producing one jar or sachet
C) The selling price of one jar
D) The profit made from one jar
quiz.explanation: Unit cost is the total cost to produce a single unit, including ingredients, packaging, labour, and overheads allocated per unit.

quiz.q: If a batch of 50 jars costs 19,950 CFA, what is the unit cost per jar?
options: A) 399 CFA
B) 400 CFA
C) 420 CFA
D) 500 CFA
quiz.explanation: 19,950 divided by 50 equals 399 CFA per jar.

quiz.q: Why should you add a small amount for spoilage or wastage when calculating unit cost?
options: A) To increase your profit margin
B) To cover the cost of ingredients that spoil or are wasted
C) To pay taxes
D) To reduce the selling price
quiz.explanation: Spoilage and wastage are real costs, so adding a percentage ensures your price covers them.

quiz.q: What is cost-plus pricing?
options: A) Setting price based only on competitor prices
B) Adding a desired profit margin to the unit cost
C) Selling at the lowest possible price
D) Pricing based on customer income
quiz.explanation: Cost-plus pricing means calculating your unit cost and then adding a percentage for profit.

quiz.q: If unit cost is 420 CFA and you want a 30% profit margin, what is the selling price?
options: A) 450 CFA
B) 500 CFA
C) 546 CFA
D) 600 CFA
quiz.explanation: 420 multiplied by 1.30 equals 546 CFA.

quiz.q: Why is it important to check competitor prices when setting your selling price?
options: A) To copy their price exactly
B) To ensure your price is not too high or too low for the market
C) To force them out of business
D) To increase your costs
quiz.explanation: Competitor prices help you gauge what customers are willing to pay and adjust your margin accordingly.

quiz.q: What should you do if your unit cost is higher than the market price allows for a profit?
options: A) Sell at a loss
B) Reduce costs or find a different market segment
C) Borrow money to cover losses
D) Increase the price above market
quiz.explanation: You must either lower your costs or target customers who will pay a higher price.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a simple tool for keeping records?
options: A) A computer with accounting software
B) An exercise book and pen
C) A mobile phone app only
D) A calculator only
quiz.explanation: An exercise book and pen are accessible and sufficient for basic record keeping.

quiz.q: What should you record in the sales section of your record book?
options: A) Date, quantity sold, amount received
B) Only the total amount at the end of the month
C) Customer names and phone numbers
D) Your personal expenses
quiz.explanation: Recording date, quantity, and amount for each sale helps track daily performance.

quiz.q: Why is it important to separate business and personal money?
options: A) To avoid paying taxes
B) To accurately know your business profit or loss
C) To hide money from family
D) To qualify for loans
quiz.explanation: Mixing funds makes it impossible to calculate true business profit and can lead to cash shortages.

quiz.q: What is cash flow?
options: A) The total profit made in a year
B) The movement of money in and out of the business
C) The amount of stock in the store
D) The value of equipment owned
quiz.explanation: Cash flow refers to the timing and amount of cash inflows and outflows.

quiz.q: Why can a profitable business run out of cash?
options: A) Because profit is not the same as cash
B) Because they spend too much on marketing
C) Because they have too many customers
D) Because they pay taxes
quiz.explanation: Profit is an accounting figure; cash flow depends on when sales are collected and expenses paid.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a good cash flow management practice?
options: A) Selling everything on credit
B) Keeping a cash reserve for emergencies
C) Spending all cash on personal items
D) Buying unlimited stock
quiz.explanation: A cash reserve ensures you can cover unexpected expenses or buy materials when needed.

quiz.q: What is a cash flow forecast?
options: A) A list of expected cash inflows and outflows for a future period
B) A record of past sales
C) A plan to increase prices
D) A list of debts owed to you
quiz.explanation: A cash flow forecast helps you predict cash shortages or surpluses.

quiz.q: What is the break-even point?
options: A) The number of units sold to cover all costs
B) The point where you make maximum profit
C) The price at which you sell
D) The total fixed costs
quiz.explanation: Break-even is when total revenue equals total costs, resulting in zero profit or loss.

quiz.q: If selling price is 550 CFA and variable cost per unit is 420 CFA, what is the contribution margin?
options: A) 130 CFA
B) 420 CFA
C) 550 CFA
D) 970 CFA
quiz.explanation: Contribution margin is selling price minus variable cost: 550 - 420 = 130 CFA.

quiz.q: If fixed costs are 50,000 CFA and contribution margin per jar is 130 CFA, how many jars must you sell to break even?
options: A) 130 jars
B) 385 jars
C) 500 jars
D) 650 jars
quiz.explanation: 50,000 divided by 130 equals approximately 385 jars.

quiz.q: What does a break-even calculation help you determine?
options: A) The minimum sales needed to avoid a loss
B) The maximum profit possible
C) The best ingredients to use
D) The number of employees to hire
quiz.explanation: Break-even tells you the sales volume required to cover all costs.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a fixed cost for a tomato paste business?
options: A) Cost of tomatoes
B) Monthly rent for a kitchen
C) Cost of jars
D) Fuel for cooking
quiz.explanation: Rent does not change with the number of jars produced, so it is a fixed cost.

quiz.q: Why should you review your break-even point regularly?
options: A) Because costs and prices change over time
B) Because customers change
C) Because it is required by law
D) Because it is fun
quiz.explanation: Changes in ingredient prices, rent, or selling price affect your break-even point.

quiz.q: What is a common money mistake in food processing?
options: A) Separating business and personal money
B) Underpricing products by ignoring some costs
C) Keeping daily records
D) Saving for emergencies
quiz.explanation: Underpricing occurs when you forget to include all costs like fuel and labour in your unit cost.

quiz.q: Why is buying too much stock a mistake?
options: A) It ties up cash and may lead to spoilage
B) It increases your profit
C) It reduces your fixed costs
D) It attracts more customers
quiz.explanation: Excess stock can spoil and also locks cash that could be used for other needs.

quiz.q: What should you do if you sell on credit?
options: A) Forget about it
B) Set clear payment terms and follow up
C) Charge no interest
D) Only sell to friends
quiz.explanation: Following up ensures you collect the money and maintain cash flow.

quiz.q: Why should you save at least 5% of sales each week?
options: A) To pay taxes
B) For emergencies and reinvestment
C) To buy personal items
D) To lend to friends
quiz.explanation: Savings provide a buffer for unexpected expenses and can be used to grow the business.

quiz.q: What is a risk of not tracking break-even?
options: A) You might be busy but still losing money
B) You might sell too much
C) You might have too much profit
D) You might hire too many workers
quiz.explanation: Without break-even analysis, you may not realize you are operating at a loss.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a good record-keeping practice?
options: A) Recording only sales, not expenses
B) Keeping all receipts in a safe place
C) Recording only when you remember
D) Using a different book each week
quiz.explanation: Receipts provide proof of expenses and help in accurate accounting.

quiz.q: What is the formula for break-even in units?
options: A) Fixed costs Ã· (Selling price - Variable cost)
B) Fixed costs Ã Selling price
C) Variable cost Ã· Selling price
D) Total costs Ã· Number of units
quiz.explanation: Break-even units = Fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit.

quiz.q: If you want to increase your profit without raising prices, what can you do?
options: A) Reduce variable costs
B) Increase fixed costs
C) Sell on credit
D) Buy more stock
quiz.explanation: Lowering variable costs increases contribution margin, thus profit.

quiz.q: Why is it important to pay yourself a salary from the business?
options: A) To separate personal and business finances
B) To avoid paying taxes
C) To increase business expenses
D) To reduce profit
quiz.explanation: A salary clarifies personal income and prevents mixing funds, aiding record keeping.

quiz.q: What is one benefit of keeping good records?
options: A) You can get loans from microfinance institutions
B) You can avoid all taxes
C) You can sell at higher prices
D) You can hire more staff
quiz.explanation: Lenders require records to assess your business's creditworthiness.
